title: Choosing a model
objectives: say what a bigger model actually buys you
trade quality against speed and cost
cap a reply with max_tokens and notice when it is cut off
pick a model for a given job

steps.instruction: There is never one model. There is a lineup, and they are not the same tool.

rows: most things most of the time
hard reasoning, long chains of steps

body: Bigger models reason better through hard, multi-step problems.
That is the only thing they reliably win at. They are not more truthful and not less likely to invent.
For a tagging job or a tidy-up, the small one is just as right and ten times cheaper.
steps.keypoint: Bigger buys reasoning. It does not buy honesty.

steps.instruction: The cheapest model in the lineup. What does it print?
steps.after: The cheapest model in the lineup got that completely right.
steps.why: The small model gets this completely right. Reaching for a bigger one would cost more and change nothing.

steps.instruction: So reaching for the biggest model every time is the common beginner mistake.
body: It is slower, so your app feels worse.
It costs more, so you notice at exactly the moment people start using it.
And on an easy question it returns the same answer the cheap one did.
steps.keypoint: Start small. Move up only where the output is visibly worse.

steps.instruction: Deal each job to the model it needs.

items.text: tag a note with one of five labels
find the bug in 200 lines and explain the fix
fix the spelling in a sentence
turn a date into a friendlier phrase

steps.after: The split is not important versus unimportant. It is one step versus many steps.
steps.keypoint: Many steps of reasoning, go big. One step, go small.
skills: pick a model for a job

steps.instruction: Speed is not a detail. It is the feature.
body: A tag suggestion that takes six seconds will not be used twice.
The same suggestion in under a second feels like part of the app.
Nobody thanks you for the smarter model they gave up waiting for.
steps.keypoint: Latency is a product decision, not a technical one.

steps.instruction: The other dial is how much it is allowed to say.
body: max_tokens is a hard ceiling on the reply, counted in tokens.
Hit it and the reply stops mid-word. It does not summarise, it does not wrap up.
stop_reason tells you which happened: end_turn finished, max_tokens was cut off.
steps.keypoint: max_tokens is a guillotine, not a target.

steps.instruction: max_tokens is 2. What does the text look like?
steps.after: Eight characters, stopped mid-word. Never show this to a user without checking stop_reason first.
opts: The capital of Canada is Ottawa.
steps.why: Two tokens is about eight characters, and it stops there. Mid-word, no warning, no tidy ending.

steps.instruction: So you check stop_reason before showing anything.
steps.after: One check, and a half-sentence never reaches a user.
body: end_turn means it finished. Anything else means what you have is incomplete.

steps.instruction: Your app suggests a tag on every keystroke. Which model, and why?
steps.code: const perKeystroke = { model: "?", max_tokens: 5, messages: [{ role: "user", content: "tag: meeting notes" }] };
opts: large, because tagging should be accurate
small, because it runs constantly and the job is one step
large, because it is the newest
steps.why: On every keystroke, cost and speed dominate everything else. Tagging is a single-step job, which is exactly what the small model is for.
steps.after: Volume decides more often than difficulty does.
steps.keypoint: High volume plus a simple job means the cheap model, every time.

steps.instruction: Complete a request for a short, high-volume job.
steps.after: Small model, small cap. A one-word answer does not need room for an essay.
steps.keypoint: Match the cap to the answer you actually want.

steps.instruction: Routing by job is how an app stays cheap without feeling cheap.
steps.after: Routing by job is how a real app keeps the bill sane without feeling cheap.
body: One function, called everywhere. Change the routing in one place later.

steps.after: Cheapest model in the lineup, right answer, and your app stayed fast.
body: Cheapest model, right answer, and the app stayed fast.
